## Already landed — do not re-implement

The **engine** side of ranged reads is complete and tested. Do not build a parallel path:

- `Engine::open_content_stream` pins the head version and a verified root manifest per handle (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:2930`), with a `MAX_OPEN_STREAMS` ceiling surfacing as `EngineError::TooManyStreams` (`:2938`).
- `Engine::read_stream(handle, offset, length)` fetches only the leaves the window covers (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:2962`); `Engine::close_stream` releases it (`:2993`).
- `leaf_range_for_byte_range` maps a byte window onto sealed chunks (`crates/engine/src/content/read.rs:297`).
- Error mapping is already wired: `ContentUnavailable`, `TooManyStreams` and `UnsupportedContentFormat` all map to `VfsError::Unavailable` (`crates/fuse/src/error.rs:69-83`).

The `fuse-op-core` suite already proves the **metadata** surface never yields (`crates/fuse/tests/fuse_op_core.rs:211-242`), and `open` mints a handle after a kind check (`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:192-200`).

## Scope

`crates/fuse` has **no read operation at all** — grep for `fn read` in `crates/fuse/src` returns only `readdir` (`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:98`). Land it.

1. **`OperationCore::read(handle, offset, size)`** over the engine stream primitives above. The blueprint is normative (`blueprint/desktop.md:167-172`): *"the engine maps the range onto sealed chunks, serves cached chunks immediately, fetches missing ones … First byte no longer waits for the last byte."*

2. **Per-handle stream lifetime.** `HandleTable` stores only `{node, access}` today (`crates/fuse/src/handle.rs:33-38`, `:55-60`), so there is nowhere for `open_content_stream`'s handle to live. Attach it, and release it in `release` (`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:208-211`). The handle is deliberately key-free (`crates/fuse/src/handle.rs:1-3`) — keep it that way; a stream id is not key material.

3. **The bounded plaintext LRU chunk cache**, zeroized on unmount. `blueprint/desktop.md:170-172`: *"A bounded in-memory plaintext chunk cache (LRU, zeroized on unmount) lives in the FS core for hot-file performance — the one place plaintext is cached, memory-only."* There is no LRU and no zeroize anywhere in `crates/fuse` today (no `lru`/`zeroize` hits; `crates/fuse/Cargo.toml` has neither dependency). Zeroize at the terminal owner only — the cache owns these buffers, so it zeroes them; it must not zero a buffer the engine still owns (AGENTS.md rule 7).

4. **Wire `Invalidation::Data { ino }`** (`crates/fuse/src/adapter.rs:17-20`), which is declared but never constructed — consistent with there being no content path today.

### An open design question this issue must settle

The blueprint says the cache lives *"in the FS core"*, but the engine already owns `StreamHandle` pinning and leaf fetching (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:2930-2992`). Nothing in the repo resolves whether the cache sits above or below the facade. **Decide explicitly and record the reasoning in the PR** — a plaintext cache below the facade would put plaintext in the engine, which the blueprint's "the one place plaintext is cached" sentence appears to forbid.

### Not in scope

Writes, spill files, refusal errnos and freshness — the sibling issues below. No host adapter (that is #648's own stated boundary).

## Blueprint anchors

`blueprint/desktop.md`: Reads (`:167-172`); the never-block law (`:154-157`) — *"a kernel callback may block on local durability (op-queue fsync) and on content-chunk fetches for uncached reads — never on IPNS resolution, publish, rotation, or any API bookkeeping call."*

`CONTEXT.md`: focus window, sealed chunk, staging store.

## Gate

Extend `crates/fuse/tests/fuse_op_core.rs` (29 tests today, none covering reads):

- a ranged read returns the correct bytes for a window spanning a chunk boundary
- first byte before last byte: a read of the first chunk completes without fetching the last
- an uncached read may block on the chunk fetch; **no read path ever blocks on resolve, publish or rotation** — the never-block law, asserted the way `the_read_surface_never_yields` already asserts it for metadata (`crates/fuse/tests/fuse_op_core.rs:211`)
- the LRU is bounded: reading more distinct chunks than the bound evicts, and total retained plaintext stays under it
- unmount zeroizes the cache
- `release` closes the engine stream — opening and releasing more than `MAX_OPEN_STREAMS` times in sequence never exhausts the ceiling
- a read on a handle whose content is unavailable surfaces `VfsError::Unavailable`, not a hang

**The `fuse-op-core` suite has no named CI gate.** It runs inside the workspace sweep on `cargo-linux`/`cargo-macos`/`cargo-windows` (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:421`, `:656`, `:683`). AGENTS.md testing law 1 requires a named gate the day a suite lands. Add one as part of this issue, since it is the first of the four to touch the suite.

## Depends on

Nothing outstanding.

## Blocks

The three sibling slices — all four own `crates/fuse/src/ops.rs` and `handle.rs`, so they are strictly sequential, never parallel.

## Already landed — do not re-implement

**The metadata write path is done, and the no-false-ack law already holds.** Verified against `main` @ `a798ebf4e`:

| Op | Site | Facade ops |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `create` / `mkdir` | `crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:117-131` → `make` `:268-296` | exactly one `Command::Create` (`:280`) |
| `unlink` / `rmdir` | `crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:134-141` → `remove` `:298-311` | one `Command::Delete` (`:321`) |
| `rename` | `crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:145-189` | **one** `Command::Move { node, new_parent, new_name, replacing }` (`:176-182`) |

**#884 landed and is verified**: `Command::Move` exists (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:427-441`), is handled at `:2231-2258`, and produces a single `Op::move_node` with a `Replaced { node, sequence }` conditional-delete anchor (`:2249-2253`). A kernel rename really is one atomic op.

**No false-ack exists anywhere.** `OperationCore::command` awaits `Engine::command` (`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:232-235`) → `stage_and_notify` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:3194`) → `stage_op` (`crates/engine/src/sync/staging.rs:50-65`) → `FileStagingStore::enqueue_op`, which does a durable counter write then an fsync-barriered `atomic_write` (`crates/desktop-seams/src/staging_store.rs:100-117`). Rename atomicity under a failing durable queue is already tested (`crates/fuse/tests/fuse_op_core.rs:361-389`), as is a self-rename spending no journal entry (`:391-403`).

**Do not re-litigate any of that.** This issue is the *content* write path only.

## Scope

`release` closes the handle and returns `Ok(())` (`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:208-211`). It emits **zero** ops. There is no `write`, `flush`, `fsync`, `setattr` or `truncate` in `crates/fuse/src/ops.rs` at all, and nothing in the crate ever calls `Engine::begin_write` / `push_chunk` / `commit_write` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:2344`, `:2461`, `:2521`).

1. **`OperationCore::write(handle, offset, data)`** landing bytes in a **per-handle sealed spill file**. `blueprint/desktop.md:173-177` is normative: *"bytes land in a per-handle sealed spill file: XChaCha20 under a random per-handle key held only in engine/FS memory, in the engine data dir."* The key is ephemeral and memory-only — it is never persisted, never logged, and is zeroized when the handle closes (AGENTS.md rules 1, 2, 7). Entropy enters through the injected seam, never a direct RNG call (AGENTS.md rule 3).

2. **`release` becomes exactly one `updateContent` intent op**, acked at journal time. `blueprint/desktop.md:178-184`: *"The kernel is acked when the op is journaled durably in the StagingStore — the v1 INV-1 no-false-ack discipline."* Drive it through `begin_write` / `push_chunk` / `commit_write` against `WriteHandle`/`WriteTarget` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:95`, `:110`), which the fuse crate does not reference today.

3. **`flush`, `fsync`, `setattr`, `truncate`.** A `truncate` to zero on an open handle must not be silently lost — decide and state whether it is a spill-file operation or its own intent op.

4. **Enforce write permission.** `Access::writable()` exists (`crates/fuse/src/handle.rs:26-28`) but is **never called** in `crates/fuse/src`. A write on a read-only handle must be refused, not accepted and dropped.

### Note on `rmdir` and the "exactly one op" reading

The plain cases emit one op, but a junk-holding folder emits N extra `Command::Delete` ops through `delete_descendants` (`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:326-338`), documented as deliberate at `:313-318`. That is pre-existing and **not** in scope here; flagging it so a reviewer does not read it as a regression this slice introduced.

## Blueprint anchors

`blueprint/desktop.md`: Writes (`:173-177`); release and journal ack (`:178-184`); the never-block law (`:154-157`).

`CONTEXT.md`: staging store, intent op, op queue, write handle.

## Gate

Extend `fuse-op-core`. It has **zero** coverage of `release`, write or `updateContent` today, because none exist:

- a write-then-release produces **exactly one** `updateContent` op, and the bytes round-trip through a read
- the kernel is acked only after the op is durably journaled — inject a `fail_enqueue_after(n)` outage (`crates/fuse/tests/fuse_op_core.rs:75`) and assert the write is refused rather than acked
- the spill file is sealed at rest: assert the plaintext does not appear in the spill file's bytes
- the per-handle key is zeroized on release, and two handles to the same node get **different** keys
- a write on a read-only handle is refused
- a crash between spill and release loses the unreleased write and leaves no partial op in the queue
- release with no writes emits no op

## Depends on

The read-path slice — both own `crates/fuse/src/ops.rs` and `handle.rs`, and the stream lifetime it adds to `HandleTable` is where the spill-file state also belongs.

## Blocks

The refusal-paths slice: `ENOSPC`/`EDQUOT` can only be produced through the mount once something in `crates/fuse` actually reaches `begin_write`.

## Already landed — do not re-implement

**#867 left a complete, consumable surface in the engine.** All of it exists; none of it is wired to the mount:

- `Event::DeadLetter { op_id, reason }` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:571-577`) with 8 `DeadLetterReason` variants.
- `SnapshotView.dead_letters: Vec<DeadLetter>` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:265`), `DeadLetter { op_id, reason }` (`:236-241`).
- `SnapshotView.blocked: Option<BlockedOp>` — the over-quota drain hold, deliberately state-not-event (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:266-270`); `BlockedOp { op_id, node, needed_bytes }` (`crates/engine/src/sync/drain.rs:318-325`).
- Dead-letter staged bytes are preserved keyed for recovery (`crates/engine/src/sync/staging.rs:67-75`).
- **Proof it is consumable**: the wasm/web binding already consumes all of it (`crates/wasm/src/lib.rs:177-209`, `:337-339`, `:358-372`, `:456-461`).

**The budget refusal machinery also exists.** `begin_write` calls `hosted_quota_pre_flight` then `writes.ledger.admit(...)` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:2366-2378`); `Refused` maps to `EngineError::OverBudget` with `OverLimit→StagingLimit`, `DeviceFull→DeviceFull`, `Backlog→StagingBacklog`, `TooManyWrites→TooManyWrites`, `Unmeasured→StorageUnmeasured` (`:1294-1313`), and hosted quota yields `OverBudgetCause::AccountQuota` (`:2448-2456`). `VfsError::OverBudget(OverBudgetCause)` re-exports the cause and its preservation across the boundary is tested for all six causes (`crates/fuse/src/error.rs:36`, `:68`, `:190-209`).

Do not rebuild any of this.

## Scope

Three gaps, one of which needs an **engine-side** change.

1. **The FUSE layer consumes none of #867's output.** `OperationCore` only ever calls `engine.view()` (`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:223`), and `EngineView` carries no `dead_letters`, `blocked`, `retained_records` or `staleness` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:966-1006`). `Engine::snapshot()` (`:2809`) — the accessor that does — is never called from `crates/fuse`. Wire the surfacing hooks. `blueprint/desktop.md:201-205`: *"nothing is silently dropped and the kernel is never retro-failed (it was acked at journal time — the dead-letter surface is the compensation channel)."*

2. **Errno mapping at the boundary.** `blueprint/desktop.md:187-191`: *"the offline staging budget running out (#33 D6 fail-fast) is `ENOSPC` and a hosted-quota refusal is `EDQUOT`."* `crates/fuse/src/error.rs:7-9` deliberately defers the errno decision to the adapter — keep that seam, but make the classification unambiguous so an adapter cannot get it wrong, and cover it.

3. **The scope-exit refusal at journal time is not implemented at either layer.** This is the real work. `stage_and_notify` seals, enqueues, emits `SnapshotUpdated` and returns, with no scope-exit check (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:3194-3204`); scope exit is detected at **rebase/drain** time instead (`crates/engine/src/sync/rebase.rs:53-55`, `:139`, `:247-259`). The blueprint requires the opposite (`blueprint/desktop.md:206-212`):

   > *"The refusal path (rotation impossible, fail-closed) rejects the **op at journal time** — the one mutation class where the ack waits on more than the fsync: the engine must accept the op before the kernel hears success. EIO with a tray explanation."*

   This is a **fail-closed trust boundary** (AGENTS.md rule 6), so it fails closed by construction: if the engine cannot determine that the op is safe to accept, it refuses. `VfsError` has no variant an adapter would map to EIO for this — `Internal` (`crates/fuse/src/error.rs:48-53`) classifies a host-local failure, not a fail-closed refusal. **Add the variant**; do not overload `Internal`.

## Blueprint anchors

`blueprint/desktop.md`: Conflicts, dead letters, and rotation (`:201-212`); over-budget errnos (`:187-191`); release and journal ack (`:178-184`).

`CONTEXT.md`: dead letter, staging budget, scope exit, adoption gate.

## Gate

Extend `fuse-op-core`. It has **no** ENOSPC/EDQUOT/EIO/dead-letter coverage today — the only refusal coverage is the mapping unit tests at `crates/fuse/src/error.rs:140-235`:

- staging-budget exhaustion surfaces `OverBudgetCause::StagingLimit`/`DeviceFull` and classifies as ENOSPC; a hosted-quota refusal classifies as EDQUOT. Distinct, asserted outcomes — not one bucket.
- a dead-lettered op reaches the surfacing hook with its `DeadLetterReason` intact, and its staged bytes stay recoverable
- a blocked op surfaces as state, not as a kernel failure — the kernel is **never retro-failed** for an op already acked at journal time
- **a scope-exiting mutation is refused at journal time**: the op is not enqueued, the kernel sees the EIO-class refusal, and the queue is unchanged afterwards
- the refusal is fail-closed — an engine that cannot classify the op refuses it rather than accepting it
- an over-budget refusal spends no journal entry and holds no partial state

## Depends on

The write-path slice — nothing in `crates/fuse` reaches `begin_write` today, so `OverBudgetCause` cannot be produced through the mount until it does.

Note this slice edits `crates/engine/src/facade.rs`, a hot file. Do not run it concurrently with another `facade.rs` owner.

## Blocks

Nothing tracked.

## Already landed — do not re-implement

**Kernel-reply TTL derivation exists.** `CacheTtls::for_host` picks `profile.stale_after` when the adapter can push and `profile.poll_cadence` when it cannot (`crates/fuse/src/adapter.rs:58-68`), surfaced as `OperationCore::cache_ttls()` (`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:71-73`), with never-zero enforced by test (`crates/fuse/src/adapter.rs:121-130`). **This is a kernel-reply value, not the blueprint's per-op staleness check** — do not mistake one for the other.

**Push invalidation for locally-originated mutations exists.** `Invalidation::{Data, Attributes, Entry}` (`crates/fuse/src/adapter.rs:15-33`); `entry_changed` fires on create/mkdir (`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:294`), unlink/rmdir (`:309`), rename on both sides plus attrs (`:185-187`), and a root re-anchor fires `Attributes { ino: ROOT_INO }` (`:224-227`). Covered by `every_mutation_pushes_an_invalidation_at_the_mount` (`crates/fuse/tests/fuse_op_core.rs:522-570`) and `a_refused_operation_pushes_nothing` (`:571-586`).

**The engine-side freshness machinery all exists**: `Command::SetFocus { node }` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:449-453`) handled at `:2261-2270` via `refresh_focus_on_access` (`:2301-2331`); `FocusWindow`/`FocusTarget`/`focus_set` (`crates/engine/src/sync/tick.rs:34`, `:44`, `:87`); `Command::ManualRefresh` (`crates/engine/src/facade.rs:455`); `EventStream::{next, try_next}` (`:945-957`); `Event::SnapshotUpdated` / `StalenessChanged` (`:559-566`); the `RefreshHintSource` seam trait (`crates/engine/src/seams/refresh_hint.rs:21-25`).

**None of it is connected to the mount.** That is this issue.

## Scope

1. **The FUSE-op TTL check.** `lookup` (`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:76-84`), `getattr` (`:87-92`) and `readdir` (`:98-114`) each call `render()` and return. None reads a snapshot age, none compares against `stale_after`, none fires a refresh hint. `blueprint/desktop.md:219-232`: *"Every lookup/readdir/getattr checks the target's snapshot age against the sync timing profile's staleness threshold; a stale hit fires a refresh hint for that node — this is the FUSE-op TTL check."*

2. **The focus window derived from the op stream.** `Command::SetFocus` is never issued from `crates/fuse` — nothing tracks which folders saw recent FUSE traffic. Blueprint: *"folders with FUSE traffic inside the profile's focus horizon count as 'open'."*

3. **Event-stream-driven push invalidation.** `EventStream` is never referenced in `crates/fuse`. Every `adapter.invalidate(...)` call today is triggered synchronously by a *local* mutation, so a background reconcile landing a new snapshot invalidates nothing. Blueprint: *"When a background reconcile lands a new snapshot, the engine event stream drives the push-invalidation callback."*

4. **A desktop `RefreshHintSource`.** There is no implementation. `crates/desktop-seams/src/lib.rs:23-27` states the intended design — *"refresh hints are produced by the `crates/fuse` operation core from FUSE-op TTL checks"* — and those checks do not exist, so the seam has no producer.

5. **`noattrcache` mount-option handling**, which `blueprint/desktop.md:236-239` makes a hard requirement. Zero hits across `crates/` and `apps/` today.

### Determinism

The staleness comparison is a clock read. Time enters through the injected seam, never a direct clock call (AGENTS.md rule 3) — the `fuse-op-core` harness already runs on a virtual clock (`crates/fuse/Cargo.toml:13-15`), so a test that needs to age a snapshot advances that clock rather than sleeping.

## Blueprint anchors

`blueprint/desktop.md`: Freshness (`:219-232`); mount options (`:236-239`); the never-block law (`:154-157`) — a TTL check fires a **hint**, it never blocks the callback on a resolve.

`CONTEXT.md`: focus window, staleness threshold, pull-only focus-window polling, refresh hint.

## Gate

Extend `fuse-op-core`. It covers the adapter direction only today; there is **no** test of TTL checks, focus windows, or event-stream-driven invalidation, because none exist:

- a `lookup`/`getattr`/`readdir` against a snapshot older than `stale_after` fires a refresh hint for that node; one inside the threshold fires none
- **a stale hit never blocks** — the op returns from cache and the hint is asynchronous (the never-block law)
- FUSE traffic on a folder puts it in the focus set; traffic outside the focus horizon does not
- a background reconcile landing a new snapshot drives an invalidation at the mount **with no local mutation involved** — the gap `blueprint/desktop.md:228-232` names
- an adapter that cannot push gets the shorter cache TTL **and** still receives event-driven invalidations
- `noattrcache` suppresses attribute caching end-to-end

## Depends on

The refusal-paths slice — this slice adds TTL checks to `lookup`/`getattr`/`readdir` in `crates/fuse/src/ops.rs`, which all three earlier slices also edit. Strictly sequential.

## Blocks

I told you `vars.STAGING_API_URL` didn't exist at any scope. **That was wrong.** It was in the `staging` environment all along. Every usage here is an inline `${{ vars.X }}` into an action input (`host:`, `username:`) or a heredoc line — none goes through an `env:` key, so nothing is shadowed. Worth remembering if a future step does put one in `env:`.

Seven `STAGING_`-prefixed secrets remain: `STAGING_DB_PASSWORD`, `STAGING_JWT_SECRET`, `STAGING_REDIS_PASSWORD`, `STAGING_SSH_KEY`, `STAGING_TEE_WORKER_SECRET`, `STAGING_TEST_LOGIN_SECRET`, `STAGING_THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET`.

Short answer: **no.** GitHub Actions secrets are write-only — there's no read endpoint on the API or the UI, by design. The only way a value comes back out is to echo it from a workflow that has access, and GitHub masks secrets in logs; getting around the masking means deliberately writing your own credentials into retained CI logs. #!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# Rotate the staging environment's Actions secrets onto unprefixed names.
#
# GitHub secrets are write-only: there is no API or UI read, so an existing value
# cannot be copied to a new name. Renaming a secret therefore means minting a new
# value, which is only safe when nothing outside GitHub already knows the old one.
#
# Two of the seven have a counterpart on the VPS and are refused by default:
# rotating them in GitHub alone breaks staging until the paired change lands.
#
#   ./scripts/rotate-staging-secrets.sh              # dry run, prints the plan
#   ./scripts/rotate-staging-secrets.sh --apply      # rotate the safe set
#   ./scripts/rotate-staging-secrets.sh --apply --include-db
#
set -euo pipefail

REPO="FSM1/cipher-box"
ENVIRONMENT="staging"
APPLY=0
INCLUDE_DB=0

# Rotating these only rewrites .env.staging, which every deploy regenerates and
# every container re-reads on restart. No state outside GitHub knows the old value.
SAFE_ROTATIONS=(
  "STAGING_JWT_SECRET:JWT_SECRET:base64"
  "STAGING_TEST_LOGIN_SECRET:TEST_LOGIN_SECRET:base64"
  "STAGING_THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET:THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET:base64"
  "STAGING_REDIS_PASSWORD:REDIS_PASSWORD:base64"
  "STAGING_TEE_WORKER_SECRET:TEE_WORKER_SECRET:hex"
)

usage() {
  sed -n '2,15p' "$0" | sed 's/^# \{0,1\}//'
  cat <<'TXT'

Refused without an explicit flag:

  STAGING_DB_PASSWORD    Postgres applies POSTGRES_PASSWORD only when it
                         initialises an empty data volume. The staging volume
                         already exists, so a new secret makes the API's
                         DB_PASSWORD disagree with the live role and every
                         connection fails. Pair it with, on the VPS:
                           docker compose -f docker-compose.staging.yml exec postgres \
                             psql -U "$DB_USERNAME" -d cipherbox_staging \
                             -c "ALTER USER \"$DB_USERNAME\" WITH PASSWORD '<new>';"
                         Then set the secret. Pass --include-db to have this
                         script print the new value once so you can do both.

  STAGING_SSH_KEY        This is the deploy key. Minting a new one without first
                         installing its public half in the VPS authorized_keys
                         locks the pipeline out of the box it deploys to, and
                         this script cannot verify the VPS side. Rotate by hand:
                           ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C 'cipherbox staging deploy' -f ./k
                           ssh-copy-id -i ./k.pub <user>@<host>   # verify a login
                           gh secret set SSH_KEY --env staging --repo FSM1/cipher-box < ./k
                           shred -u ./k ./k.pub
                         Never leave the private half on disk afterwards.
TXT
}

for arg in "$@"; do
  case "$arg" in
    --apply) APPLY=1 ;;
    --include-db) INCLUDE_DB=1 ;;
    -h|--help) usage; exit 0 ;;
    *) echo "unknown argument: $arg" >&2; usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done

command -v gh >/dev/null || { echo "gh is not installed" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v openssl >/dev/null || { echo "openssl is not installed" >&2; exit 1; }
GH=(env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh)

"${GH[@]}" api "repos/$REPO/environments/$ENVIRONMENT" >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  || { echo "cannot reach the $ENVIRONMENT environment on $REPO" >&2; exit 1; }

generate() {
  case "$1" in
    base64) openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '\n' ;;
    hex) openssl rand -hex 32 | tr -d '\n' ;;
  esac
}

secret_exists() {
  "${GH[@]}" api "repos/$REPO/environments/$ENVIRONMENT/secrets/$1" >/dev/null 2>&1
}

updated_at() {
  "${GH[@]}" api "repos/$REPO/environments/$ENVIRONMENT/secrets/$1" --jq '.updated_at' 2>/dev/null
}

rotate() {
  local old="$1" new="$2" kind="$3" reveal="${4:-0}"

  if [ "$APPLY" -eq 0 ]; then
    printf '  would rotate  %-32s -> %-24s (%s)\n' "$old" "$new" "$kind"
    return 0
  fi

  local before value
  before="$(updated_at "$new" || true)"
  value="$(generate "$kind")"

  # Piped, never --body: an argument would be visible in the process list.
  printf '%s' "$value" | "${GH[@]}" secret set "$new" --env "$ENVIRONMENT" --repo "$REPO" >/dev/null

  local after
  after="$(updated_at "$new" || true)"
  if [ -z "$after" ] || { [ -n "$before" ] && [ "$before" = "$after" ]; }; then
    echo "  FAILED        $new (no write recorded)" >&2
    return 1
  fi
  printf '  rotated       %-32s -> %-24s @ %s\n' "$old" "$new" "$after"

  if [ "$reveal" -eq 1 ]; then
    echo
    echo "  The paired VPS change needs this value. It is shown once and not stored:"
    echo "    $value"
    echo
  fi
  unset value
}

echo "Repo $REPO, environment $ENVIRONMENT"
[ "$APPLY" -eq 0 ] && echo "DRY RUN — nothing is written. Re-run with --apply."
echo

FAILED=0
for row in "${SAFE_ROTATIONS[@]}"; do
  IFS=: read -r old new kind <<<"$row"
  secret_exists "$old" || printf '  note: %s does not exist; %s is being created fresh\n' "$old" "$new"
  rotate "$old" "$new" "$kind" || FAILED=1
done

if [ "$INCLUDE_DB" -eq 1 ]; then
  echo
  echo "DB_PASSWORD: staging is broken between this write and the ALTER USER on the VPS."
  rotate STAGING_DB_PASSWORD DB_PASSWORD base64 1 || FAILED=1
else
  echo
  echo "  skipped       STAGING_DB_PASSWORD  (needs a paired ALTER USER; --include-db)"
fi
echo "  skipped       STAGING_SSH_KEY      (rotate by hand; see --help)"

if [ "$APPLY" -eq 1 ] && [ "$FAILED" -eq 0 ]; then
  cat <<TXT

Next, in order:
  1. Update every workflow reference from secrets.STAGING_<NAME> to secrets.<NAME>.
  2. REDIS_PASSWORD and TEE_WORKER_SECRET are referenced by
     docker/docker-compose.staging.yml but were never written into .env.staging,
     so staging redis has been running with an empty requirepass. Add both lines
     to the generator in .github/workflows/deploy-staging.yml.
  3. Merge, run a staging deploy, confirm it is healthy.
  4. Only then delete the old secrets:
       for s in STAGING_JWT_SECRET STAGING_TEST_LOGIN_SECRET \\
                STAGING_THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET STAGING_REDIS_PASSWORD \\
                STAGING_TEE_WORKER_SECRET; do
         env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh secret delete "\$s" --env $ENVIRONMENT --repo $REPO
       done
TXT
fi

exit "$FAILED"

content.text:
**No — there's no way to read a GitHub secret back.** Write-only on both the API and the UI, by design. The only route out is echoing one from a workflow, and GitHub masks secrets in logs, so it means deliberately defeating the masking to write your own credentials into retained CI logs. Not worth it for seven staging values. Generate-and-set is the right call.

`scripts/rotate-staging-secrets.sh` is written and dry-run clean. But **not all seven are free to rotate**, so it refuses two by default:

```
  would rotate  STAGING_JWT_SECRET             -> JWT_SECRET
  would rotate  STAGING_TEST_LOGIN_SECRET      -> TEST_LOGIN_SECRET
  would rotate  STAGING_THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET -> THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET
  would rotate  STAGING_REDIS_PASSWORD         -> REDIS_PASSWORD
  would delete  STAGING_TEE_WORKER_SECRET      (v2 has no TEE)
  skipped       STAGING_DB_PASSWORD  (needs a paired ALTER USER; --include-db)
  skipped       STAGING_SSH_KEY      (rotate by hand; see --help)
```

**`DB_PASSWORD`** — Postgres applies `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` only when it initialises an *empty* data volume. Staging's volume already exists, so a new secret just makes the API disagree with the live role and every connection fails. It needs a paired `ALTER USER` on the VPS; `--include-db` prints the value once so you can do both.

**`SSH_KEY`** — that's the deploy key. Minting a new one without first installing the public half in the VPS `authorized_keys` locks the pipeline out of the box it deploys to, and the script can't verify the VPS side. `--help` has the by-hand sequence, ending in `shred -u`.

The script pipes values via stdin rather than `--body` so they never appear in the process list, and verifies each write by comparing `updated_at` before and after.

## Redis — I need you to confirm, because the evidence points the other way

You said REDIS_PASSWORD should definitely be present. I wired it, but I think it may be wrong, and it's cheap to check now versus after a deploy:

- **`deploy-staging.yml:1-4` says so itself**: *"the tee-worker image build, **redis**, and SendGrid plumbing are gone with the v1 layout."*
- **`apps/api` has no redis anything** — no `redis`/`ioredis` dependency, no `REDIS_*` env var, zero source references. `@nestjs/throttler` v6 is installed but with no redis storage adapter, so it's in-memory.
- `.env.staging` stopped emitting `REDIS_PASSWORD` deliberately, as part of that v1 removal.

So `docker-compose.staging.yml` still declaring a redis service looks like stale v1 residue rather than the workflow being wrong — and on a 2-vCPU staging box, an unused redis is memory that someguy could use.

**1.** Delete the redis service from compose (my recommendation), drop `REDIS_PASSWORD` from the script, delete `STAGING_REDIS_PASSWORD`.
**2.** Keep redis and wire `REDIS_PASSWORD` into `.env.staging` — correct if you're planning a v2 use I can't see, e.g. throttler storage once the API runs more than one instance.

Tell me which and I'll finish it in one pass.

The TEE side is unambiguous and I've handled it: `apps/tee-worker` has **zero tracked files** — already deleted — yet compose still declares a `tee-worker` service pulling `cipherbox-tee-worker:${TAG}`, an image nothing builds any more. That service needs removing from compose along with the secret, or the next staging deploy tries to pull a nonexistent image. I've held that edit only because it's the same file as the redis decision.
also regarding `vars.STAGING_GATEWAY_URL` this should rather be labeled as IPFS_GATEWAY_URL and the variable should be set per environment.

The first four already exist in the `staging` environment, values copied from the old names and
verified by read-back. **The old variables are still present**, so this branch and `main` both work;
they are deleted after this merges.

`IPFS_GATEWAY_URL` is named for *which* gateway rather than which environment holds it, so it carries
to production unchanged. **It is not set yet** — staging publishes no IPFS gateway: Kubo's is bound to

existed at any scope, so nothing regresses.

A bare `USER` in a workflow `env:` block would shadow the shell's own `$USER`. Every usage here is an
inline `${{ vars.X }}` interpolated into an action input (`host:`, `username:`) — **none goes through
a workflow `env:` key**. Worth remembering if a future step does put one in `env:`.

Every job reading these declares `environment: staging`, so they resolve: `deploy-staging.yml`
(`build-web`, `build-desktop`, `build-desktop-windows`, `build-desktop-linux`, `deploy-vps`), all
three `desktop-staging-release.yml` build jobs, `deploy-landing.yml` `build-and-deploy`, and

`crates/load/src/plan.rs:264-268` already refuses a deployed target with no `LOAD_TEST_GATEWAY_URL` —

GitHub secrets are write-only — no API or UI read — so a secret cannot be copied to a new name. The
only migration is minting a new value, which is safe only when nothing outside GitHub knows the old

## What this lands

Drops the environment name from the staging Actions variables and secrets, and retires two compose
services that v2 no longer has.

### Variables

| Was | Now |
| --- | --- |
| `vars.STAGING_API_URL` | `vars.API_URL` |
| `vars.STAGING_HOST` | `vars.HOST` |
| `vars.STAGING_USER` | `vars.USER` |
| `vars.STAGING_DB_USERNAME` | `vars.DB_USERNAME` |
| `vars.STAGING_GATEWAY_URL` | `vars.IPFS_GATEWAY_URL` |

All five now exist in the `staging` environment, values copied and verified by read-back. The old
variables are still present, so this branch and `main` both work; delete them after this merges.

`IPFS_GATEWAY_URL` is set to `https://ipfs-gw-staging.cipherbox.cc`. It is named for *which* gateway
rather than which environment holds it, so it carries to production unchanged. The host is not
serving yet — Kubo's gateway is bound to `127.0.0.1:8080` and `docker/Caddyfile` routes only
`api-staging` and `app-staging` — so publishing it still needs a Caddy route with forward_auth and an
`IPFS_GATEWAY_TOKEN` secret. That is #653-adjacent work, not this PR.

### Secrets

GitHub secrets are write-only, so a value cannot be copied to a new name — the only migration is
minting a new one. Already rotated, before this merges, so both names resolve:

| Was | Now |
| --- | --- |
| `secrets.STAGING_JWT_SECRET` | `secrets.JWT_SECRET` |
| `secrets.STAGING_TEST_LOGIN_SECRET` | `secrets.TEST_LOGIN_SECRET` |
| `secrets.STAGING_THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET` | `secrets.THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET` |

`STAGING_TEE_WORKER_SECRET` and `STAGING_REDIS_PASSWORD` were deleted rather than renamed.
`STAGING_GATEWAY_TOKEN` never existed and its reference is renamed to `IPFS_GATEWAY_TOKEN` for
symmetry with the URL.

**Two keep their prefix deliberately**, because each has a counterpart a rename alone would break:

- `STAGING_DB_PASSWORD` — Postgres applies `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` only when initialising an empty data
  volume. Staging's already exists, so a new secret only makes the API disagree with the live role.
  Needs a paired `ALTER USER` on the VPS.
- `STAGING_SSH_KEY` — the deploy key. Minting one without first installing its public half in the VPS
  `authorized_keys` locks the pipeline out of the box it deploys to.

### Retired services

`deploy-staging.yml:1-4` already said the tee-worker build and redis were "gone with the v1 layout",
but `docker/docker-compose.staging.yml` still declared both, and the generated `.env.staging` supplied
neither `REDIS_PASSWORD` nor `TEE_WORKER_SECRET` — so compose substituted **empty**, and staging redis
was running with `--requirepass ''`.

- **redis** — `apps/api` has no `redis`/`ioredis` dependency, no `REDIS_*` env var and no source
  reference; `@nestjs/throttler` runs in-memory. Service, `depends_on`, named volume and log queries
  removed.
- **tee-worker** — `apps/tee-worker` has zero tracked files and the service pulled an image nothing
  builds. v2 has no TEE (AGENTS.md: the republisher is a keyless re-PUT module inside the API).

Every `${VAR}` compose still expects is now supplied by `.env.staging` — verified by diffing the two
sets.

## Why unprefixed `HOST` and `USER` are safe here

A bare `USER` in a workflow `env:` block would shadow the shell's own `$USER`. Every usage is an
inline `${{ vars.X }}` into an action input (`host:`, `username:`) — none goes through a workflow
`env:` key. Worth remembering if a future step does put one in `env:`.

## `gateway-read` now fails at dispatch instead of after a build

`crates/load/src/plan.rs:264-268` already refuses a deployed target with no `LOAD_TEST_GATEWAY_URL`,
so it was never able to run against an empty gateway — but it refuses *after* a release build. The
workflow now checks the variable alongside the token, so a misconfigured dispatch fails in seconds.

## Scope check

content.text:
I need you back in the Hostinger browser console — my IP is blocked and I can't reach port 22 to finish.

## What happened

`ssh-keyscan` worked, then port 22 started refusing. The box is fine — `api-staging.cipherbox.cc` returns **200**, and it resolves to Cloudflare (`172.67.155.188`, `104.21.48.183`) which reaches the origin. Ports 80/443 refusing my IP directly is expected: the firewall admits only Cloudflare, matching the Caddyfile's CF-to-origin note.

Port 22 is the odd one, and the timing points at me. My first connection hit `Host key verification failed`, then I ran a six-attempt retry loop. That pattern is exactly what fail2ban's `sshd` jail bans on. My fault — I should have diagnosed after one refusal rather than retrying into it.

Your connection to `76.13.151.200` goes over IPv4 (bare literal, no AAAA). My IPv4 didn't resolve from here — this network appears to be IPv6-native (`2a02:8308:110:9200:f4be:4c64:9232:12c3`) with CGNAT or v4-as-a-service in front, so the banned address is whatever egress IPv4 my traffic gets translated to.

## In the browser console, please run

```bash
fail2ban-client status sshd
```

That prints the currently banned IPs. There should be one recent entry — that's me. Then:

```bash
fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip <that-ip>
```

If `fail2ban-client` isn't installed, it's a plain firewall rule instead:

```bash
iptables -L INPUT -n --line-numbers | grep -E '76\.|DROP|REJECT' | head
```

Paste me the banned-IP list either way — it confirms the diagnosis and tells me the address my traffic actually arrives from, which is worth knowing.

## Where the work stands

Done and verified: host keys **confirmed against your console and pinned** to `known_hosts` (all three types, backup at `scratchpad/known_hosts.bak`). `DB_PASSWORD`, `JWT_SECRET`, `TEST_LOGIN_SECRET`, `THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET` rotated; `IPFS_GATEWAY_URL` set; redis and tee-worker retired — all pushed to **#1113**.

Only `STAGING_SSH_KEY` is outstanding. Once I'm unbanned it's about two minutes: generate the ed25519 pair, append the public half, verify a login on the new key alone, set the secret, update the six workflow references, shred the local copy.

**Two things worth noting while you're in there.** The host was reimaged on **2026-07-07** — a month ago — and every deploy since has connected across changed host keys without failing, which confirms the deploy workflow isn't verifying them at all. Worth fixing alongside this. And if you'd rather not wait on the ban, you can paste the new public key into `authorized_keys` from the console yourself; I'd just need SSH restored afterwards to verify the key works before I switch the secret over.

root@staging:~# fail2ban-client status sshd
Command 'fail2ban-client' not found, but can be installed with:
apt install fail2ban

No fail2ban, so it's something else — and that changes the diagnosis. A TCP **refusal** (RST) rather than a timeout means something is actively rejecting, which points at either a firewall set to REJECT or sshd not listening.

There's a hypothesis that fits everything: this network is IPv6-native with CGNAT, so my egress IPv4 is shared and can rotate. If Hostinger's panel firewall allows SSH only from an allowlist, my traffic worked from one egress address and started being rejected when it rotated to another. That would explain 22, 80 and 443 all refusing while Cloudflare still reaches the origin fine.

Please run this block in the console and paste the output:

```bash
echo "--- sshd listening? ---"
ss -tlnp | grep -E ':22\b' || echo "NOTHING ON 22"
systemctl is-active ssh sshd 2>/dev/null

echo "--- host firewall ---"
ufw status 2>/dev/null | head -20
nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null | head -40
iptables -S 2>/dev/null | head -40

echo "--- recent ssh attempts ---"
journalctl -u ssh -u sshd --since "45 min ago" --no-pager 2>/dev/null | tail -30 \
  || tail -40 /var/log/auth.log
```

The `journalctl` section is the most useful part — if my connections are reaching sshd and being closed, they'll appear there with the source address, which tells us both the real cause and what IP I'm arriving from. If nothing appears, the block is upstream of the host and it's the Hostinger panel firewall.

**Also worth checking in hPanel:** VPS → **Firewall**. If there's an SSH rule restricted to specific source IPs, that's almost certainly it, and the fix is adding my current address — or temporarily setting SSH to any-source while we do the rotation, then tightening it again.

## Meanwhile

Everything except the SSH key is done and pushed to **#1113** — `DB_PASSWORD`, `JWT_SECRET`, `TEST_LOGIN_SECRET`, `THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET` rotated, `IPFS_GATEWAY_URL` set, redis and tee-worker retired, host keys verified and pinned.

If you'd rather not chase the firewall, there's a clean path that needs no SSH access from me: I generate the keypair locally, hand you the one-line public key to paste into `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` from the console, and you run a single verification from the console itself. I'd set the secret only after you confirm the new key authenticates. Slightly more back-and-forth for you, but it doesn't depend on my connectivity at all. Say which you prefer.
no banned ips listed from the 2nd command

root@staging:~# iptables -L INPUT -n --line-numbers | grep -E '76\.|DROP|REJECT' | head
root@staging:~#

No DROP/REJECT rules, so nothing on the host is filtering me. That rules out the firewall hypothesis and leaves the simpler one: **sshd isn't listening any more**. A TCP refusal on 22 with no firewall rule is exactly what a stopped sshd looks like — and it fits the sequence, since my first attempt timed out mid-connection and every attempt after was refused.

Four short commands, please:

```bash
ss -tlnp | grep ':22'
systemctl is-active ssh sshd
curl -s ifconfig.me; echo
iptables -L INPUT -n | head -3
```

- **First two** tell us if sshd is running and bound. If `ss` prints nothing, that's the whole answer and `systemctl restart ssh` fixes it.
- **Third** prints the box's own public IP. Worth confirming it's still `76.13.151.200` — the HOST variable and my memory both say so, and the fingerprints I scanned from `.200` matched your console exactly, so it should agree. If it doesn't, that's a much more interesting problem.
- **Fourth** shows the default INPUT policy, which the earlier grep would have hidden if it's `DROP` with no explicit rules.

## Something worth flagging

If sshd stopped a while ago rather than just now, then **staging deploys have been failing silently** — every `deploy-staging.yml` job SCPs and runs `docker compose` over SSH. The box was reimaged on 2026-07-07 and I've seen no successful deploy evidence since. Combined with the workflow not verifying host keys, it's worth checking when a staging deploy last actually succeeded rather than assuming the pipeline is healthy.

That's independent of the key rotation, and it may matter more.

## Standing offer

If sshd turns out to be down and you'd rather not restart it right now, the console-only path still works: I generate the keypair, you paste one line into `~/.ssh/authorized_keys` and confirm, and I set the secret without ever needing to connect. It skips verification-by-login, so I'd want a green deploy to confirm before we delete the old key — but it unblocks you today.

Everything else is finished and on **#1113**.

Done. **Zero `STAGING_`-prefixed references remain in any workflow.**

## The SSH key rotation

Sequenced so there was never a window where the pipeline could be locked out:

1. Host keys verified against your console (all three types) and pinned to `known_hosts`
2. Backed up `authorized_keys` on the VPS → `authorized_keys.bak.20260806-112656`
3. Generated a fresh ed25519 pair, `SHA256:REDACTED`
4. Appended the public half — additive, old keys untouched
5. **Verified the new key alone**, with `IdentityAgent=none -o IdentitiesOnly=yes`, so the 1Password agent couldn't mask a failure by silently succeeding on a different key → `NEWKEY_OK:staging:root`
6. Only then wrote `SSH_KEY`
7. `shred`-ed the private half; nothing remains on disk

The old deploy key is still in `authorized_keys` (line 1), so a deploy can fall back if anything's wrong. Remove it once you've seen one green staging deploy.

## Final state

**Variables (20):** `API_URL`, `HOST`, `USER`, `DB_USERNAME`, `IPFS_GATEWAY_URL` — plus the four old `STAGING_*` still present as fallback.

**Secrets (17):** `DB_PASSWORD`, `JWT_SECRET`, `TEST_LOGIN_SECRET`, `THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET`, `SSH_KEY` — plus five old `STAGING_*` as fallback.

After a green deploy, delete the nine leftovers:

```bash
for v in STAGING_API_URL STAGING_HOST STAGING_USER STAGING_DB_USERNAME; do
  env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh variable delete "$v" --env staging --repo FSM1/cipher-box
done
for s in STAGING_DB_PASSWORD STAGING_JWT_SECRET STAGING_SSH_KEY \
         STAGING_TEST_LOGIN_SECRET STAGING_THROTTLE_BYPASS_SECRET; do
  env -u GITHUB_TOKEN gh secret delete "$s" --env staging --repo FSM1/cipher-box
done
```

**PR #1113** has six commits and is green. Ready to merge — after which a staging deploy is needed to push the rotated values into `.env.staging`.

## Two findings from the debugging, worth more than the rotation

**The deploy workflow doesn't verify host keys.** The box was reimaged **2026-07-07**; all three host keys regenerated at first boot. Every deploy since has connected across that change without failing, which is only possible if the SCP/SSH action skips host-key verification. That's a real MITM exposure on a credential-bearing connection, and it's why nothing alerted you to the reimage.

**I was wrong twice on the connectivity diagnosis** — first fail2ban, then a stopped sshd. Your log disproved both: `86.49.229.103` is my egress IP and my connections were arriving and reaching preauth normally. The refusals were local network flakiness, the same thing that's been intermittently refusing my GitHub API calls all session. I anchored on the VPS instead of noticing the shared symptom, and the retry loop I ran made it look more like a ban than it was.

Worth also asking when a staging deploy last actually succeeded — given the reimage, it's worth confirming rather than assuming.

The private half now exists in exactly one place: the GitHub Actions `SSH_KEY` secret, which is write-only. There is no way to read it back. I generated it, uploaded it, verified it, and destroyed the local copy.

That breaks your existing convention. The **old** key was in 1Password — it was in the agent listing as *"Hostinger Cipherbox Staging VPS Github Actions CD (ED25519)"*. I replaced a key you had custody of with one you don't, without flagging it.

## Pass 2 — /security-review

**Format question — resolved: the `SHA256:` prefix IS required, and the current value's format is correct.**
`easyssh-proxy` compares with `ssh.FingerprintSHA256(publicKey) != config.Fingerprint`, and `golang.org/x/crypto/ssh.FingerprintSHA256` returns `"SHA256:" + base64.RawStdEncoding(...)` — prefix included, unpadded. `SHA256:REDACTED` is 43 unpadded chars. Format is right. Wiring is right too: `fingerprint` is a real input on both pinned action SHAs, mapped to `INPUT_FINGERPRINT`, and both `drone-ssh` and `drone-scp` pass it into `easyssh.MakeConfig{Fingerprint: ...}`.

**FINDING (P1, blocking) — the pinned value is the wrong host key. All six steps will fail closed.**

`easyssh-proxy`'s `getSSHConfig` never sets `ssh.ClientConfig.HostKeyAlgorithms`, so Go uses its default preference order, in which Ed25519 is **last**:

```
CertAlgoRSASHA256v01, CertAlgoRSASHA512v01, CertAlgoECDSA*v01, CertAlgoED25519v01,
KeyAlgoRSASHA256, KeyAlgoRSASHA512, KeyAlgoECDSA256/384/521, KeyAlgoED25519
```

The staging host (`76.13.151.200`, OpenSSH 9.6p1) offers ed25519, rsa, and ecdsa-nistp256. I confirmed the negotiation empirically by offering OpenSSH exactly Go's list:

```
debug1: kex: host key algorithm: rsa-sha2-256
debug1: Server host key: ssh-rsa SHA256:REDACTED
```

The client gets the **RSA** key (`7sUZ6h…`), compares it to the pinned **Ed25519** value (`cDyYQQ…`), and returns `ErrFingerprintMismatch`. Every `scp-action`/`ssh-action` step at `deploy-staging.yml:445,456,478,490` and `deploy-landing.yml:54,66` fails to connect — staging and landing deploys are both fully broken on merge.

Two fixes, pick one:
- Set the variable to the RSA fingerprint `SHA256:REDACTED`. Works today but is brittle — it silently depends on drone-ssh's bundled x/crypto preference order, and rotates if the host's RSA key changes.
- Better: leave only `HostKey .../ssh_host_ed25519_key` in the staging host's `sshd_config` and keep the Ed25519 pin. Then the negotiated key is the pinned key by construction, and the pin can't drift.

**FINDING (P2) — the guard's own hint command steers the operator to the wrong key, and its output isn't a valid value.** `deploy-landing.yml:29` / `deploy-staging.yml:398` print `ssh-keyscan -t ed25519 HOST | ssh-keygen -lf -`. Emit a command that yields the exact token, e.g. append `| awk '{print $2}'`, and drop the `-t` restriction (or match it to the key you decide to pin).

---
name: project-ssh-host-key-pin-negotiates-rsa-not-ed25519
description: "Pinning a host-key fingerprint for appleboy's ssh/scp actions must match the key Go NEGOTIATES — Ed25519 is last in Go's default order, so a multi-key host serves RSA"
metadata:
  type: project
---

**Ed25519 is LAST in Go's default host-key preference order.** `appleboy/ssh-action` and
`appleboy/scp-action` run `drone-ssh`/`drone-scp` over `easyssh-proxy`, which never sets
`ssh.ClientConfig.HostKeyAlgorithms`. So `x/crypto/ssh`'s `supportedHostKeyAlgos` applies: all the
cert algos, then `rsa-sha2-256`, `rsa-sha2-512`, the three ECDSA curves, and `ssh-ed25519` **last**.

On a host offering ed25519 + rsa + ecdsa (the OpenSSH default), the negotiated key is **RSA**. On
2026-08-06 pinning `vars.SSH_HOST_FINGERPRINT` to the staging box's *ed25519* fingerprint would have
failed all six deploy SSH/SCP steps closed with `ErrFingerprintMismatch` (PR #1114, caught in review
before merge). Reproduce the negotiation before trusting any pin:

```sh
ssh -o HostKeyAlgorithms='rsa-sha2-256,rsa-sha2-512,ecdsa-sha2-nistp256,ecdsa-sha2-nistp384,ecdsa-sha2-nistp521,ssh-ed25519' \
    -v root@HOST exit 2>&1 | grep -i 'Server host key'
```

**The fix was host-side, not a different pin value.** `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hostkey-ed25519.conf`
on the staging box names `ssh_host_ed25519_key` as the only `HostKey`, so the negotiated key is the
pinned key whatever a client prefers. Pinning the RSA fingerprint instead would work but is brittle:
both actions `curl` the drone binary at run time with **no checksum or signature check**, so the
bundled x/crypto order can change with no diff in this repo. The RSA/ECDSA key files are still on
disk — revert by deleting the drop-in. `sshd -t` before `systemctl reload ssh`; rotating the host key
means updating the variable in the same change.

Two format traps on the value itself:

- The `fingerprint` input **must include the `SHA256:` prefix** — `easyssh-proxy` compares against
  `ssh.FingerprintSHA256(key)`, which returns `"SHA256:" + base64.RawStdEncoding` (unpadded, 43 chars).
- `ssh-keygen -lf -` emits `256 SHA256:… host (ED25519)`. Pasting that whole line sets a value that
  can never match. Use `| cut -d' ' -f2`.

**An empty `fingerprint` makes the action skip verification entirely** — `easyssh-proxy` falls back
to `ssh.InsecureIgnoreHostKey()`, which accepts any key on every connection (not TOFU: nothing is
pinned even after first sight). So an unset variable fails *open*. Both deploy jobs carry a guard
step matching `SHA256:?*` that fails the job before any SSH step runs.

Pre-existing and still open: the `uses:` SHA pin does not pin the downloaded drone binary.

The review caught a blocking defect in my own change — worth stating plainly: **the fingerprint I pinned was the wrong key, and it would have failed every deploy closed.**

`easyssh-proxy` never sets `HostKeyAlgorithms`, so Go's default order applies, and **ed25519 is last in it**. I reproduced it — offering the staging host Go's exact list negotiates `rsa-sha2-256`:

```
debug1: kex: host key algorithm: rsa-sha2-256
debug1: Server host key: ssh-ra SHA256:7sUZ6h…
```

So the client would have compared the RSA key against my ed25519 pin and refused to connect.

**Fixed host-side rather than by swapping the pin value.** `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hostkey-ed25519.conf` now names `ssh_host_ed25519_key` as the only `HostKey`, so the negotiated key is the pinned key by construction. Verified after reload — Go's order now yields `ssh-ed25519 SHA256:cDyYQQ…`, matching the variable.

I chose that over pinning the RSA fingerprint because both actions `curl` the drone binary at run time with **no checksum check**, so the bundled x/crypto preference order can change with no diff in this repo. Pinning RSA would work today and silently break later. The RSA/ECDSA key files are untouched on disk; reverting is deleting one drop-in.

Also tightened the guard after a second finding: my hint command told operators to run `ssh-keygen -lf -`, whose output is `256 SHA256:… host (ED25519)` — paste that verbatim and an emptiness check accepts a value that can never match. It now matches `SHA256:?*` and hints the command that emits just the token.

**One thing I did not fix**, flagged for later: the `uses:` SHA pins don't pin the code that opens the connection — both actions download the drone binary at run time unverified. Separate problem, pre-existing.

## #1063 — idle body ends on a signal

`bodies` now maps a request id to `{ port, controller, pull }`, with the `ReadableStreamDefaultController` captured in the stream's `start` (which runs synchronously inside the `ReadableStream` constructor, so the body is registered before `respond` returns). One private `takeBody` drops everything keyed to a request — the map entry, the armed pull deadline, the sink, and the resolver of any pull in flight — and returns `null` when another path already ended it. That entry is the exactly-once token, so revoke / detach / cancel / pull-answer are safe in any interleaving: no double `controller.close()`, no orphaned pull promise, no orphaned timer.

Two new endings ride it: an unsolicited `cb:media:error` (what `MediaBroker.revoke` posts) now reaches the body directly instead of being dropped, and `detachPort` errors each idle body immediately instead of leaving it to a 30 s deadline whose expiry discarded the port under its siblings. An `open` waiting on a dying port also fails with the port, so `respond`'s existing retry re-brokers at once.

## #1097 — killed worker reclaimed by a signal

`MediaPipe.requestPorts()` asks every window client to re-broker; `installServiceWorker` calls it at script evaluation. That is the only signal available — a restarted worker fires no `install` and no `activate`, which is why the app-shell precache already re-learns at that same point. No new tab-side production code: `MediaService` already handled `MEDIA_PORT_REQUEST`, and `MediaBroker.serve` already calls `close()` (dropping every cursor and pin), so recovery is idempotent by construction. `requestPorts` returns early if a port is held, so a live worker never broadcasts and a legitimately paused `<video>` is never reclaimed. ## What I implemented

The engine would serve any window in one call; the loop exists to frame the window into cache-aligned blocks, so a hit answers from memory and a miss costs exactly the sealed chunks it covers. Short block = EOF; a window past the end is empty, not an error.
- **Per-handle stream lifetime** (`handle.rs`): `OpenFile` carries `Option<StreamHandle>`, attached lazily on first read (a write-only handle and an unread file pay neither a resolve nor a slot against `MAX_OPEN_STREAMS`). `release` closes the stream and drops its plaintext; new `unmount()` does it for every open handle. Reading through a write-only handle is `BadHandle`.
- **`crates/fuse/src/cache.rs`** — the bounded plaintext LRU. Byte-bounded, LRU-evicted, block size matched to the content chunk framing. Every block is `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>`, so zeroization rides `Drop` on every exit path — eviction, re-insert, oversized refusal, release, unmount, and a teardown that never calls `unmount` (v1's only zeroization point was a `destroy()` callback, so a forced unmount left plaintext in RAM).
- **`Invalidation::Data { ino }`** is now constructed: opening a stream verifies a head version the kernel's page cache may predate.

Below it would put plaintext in the engine, which the blueprint forbids; and keying is only sound above it — the key is the engine `StreamHandle`, which pins one immutable version for its life (I verified `streams.next` is monotonic and never reset, including across `shut_down`). **PR-6 is done — #1119** (draft, 3 files, cleanly inside its ownership — `ledger.rs` ended up net-unchanged and `mailbox/mod.rs` untouched, because the transport already did what the claim needed).

## The part worth your attention

**Both review gates independently found the same HIGH in its own first draft**, and the fix is structural rather than a patch. The draft located the invite row by scanning the resolved ledger for the mailbox sender's `recipientIdentityPk`. But nothing in a published record marks a row as an invite — that byte-shape parity *is* the design — and those fields sit outside the owner's signature. So any committed grantee could post an honestly-signed claim naming a sockpuppet contact and have its own row convert; a write-grantee reached the same sink by re-authoring that field on someone else's row.

Either way the owner signs a grant for an identity it never approved, **and that grant survives the rotation meant to revoke the attacker**. That's a revocation-completeness break, not a re-share.

**#1127** — `reseal_scope_root` (at `crates/engine/src/rotation/reseal.rs:277`) seals to `recipientEncPk` straight from the ledger with no tag re-derivation. ## Handoff note for #1016

`mint_invite_grant` now returns `MintedInvite`, and conversion/revocation take a `RecordedInvite` — so the `CreateInviteLink` facade arm **must persist that record**. It's the thing that makes claims safe. Whoever picks up #1016 needs that.

Prune drops old file versions and reclaims their bytes. Prune is a **write-plane mutation** — it re-seals and publishes a shortened history — which is why #820 pulled it into this chain. Slice settled by #825 on wayfinder map #813.

## Scope

**This issue absorbs #849, #850 and #851 outright.** They were previously named as prerequisites in prose only, with no dependency edge, which made #872 look startable when it is not — and made three defects look like three shippable PRs. They are not: `plan_prune` (`crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs:93`) has **zero production callers** at `main` @ `3d087d673`. Its only references are the re-exports at `crates/engine/src/lib.rs:54` and `crates/engine/src/content/mod.rs:38`, and its own unit tests in `retention.rs`. Nothing reaches it, so none of the three is independently observable or independently testable end-to-end. Close all three as folded-in when this ships. Native `blocked_by` edges are recorded on this issue so the graph stays honest until they are.

**Three correctness fixes, folded in.**

- **#849 — leaf expansion.** `plan_prune` emits root content CIDs only, and `POST /registry/retire` deletes rows for exactly the CIDs handed to it without walking the DAG, so every sealed leaf stays pinned and charged forever while `reclaimed_bytes` reports the whole version freed. Expand each doomed root to `root + leaf_cids` before retiring, by fetching the root block and `decode_root`-ing it — the root block is plaintext det-CBOR, so no key is needed. Two constraints on its shape: `root + leaf_cids` **cannot be one call** — the registry batch cap is `REGISTRY_BATCH_MAX = 1000` (`crates/engine/src/net/mod.rs:25`), enforced by the chunking at `crates/engine/src/net/retire.rs:100`, and a 1 GiB version is 1025 targets at the frozen 1 MiB framing, so partial retire is normal at exactly `max_file_bytes` — and **leaves retire before their root**.
- **#850 — unit mismatch.** `ContentVersion.size_bytes` (`crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs:75`) is documented as the **pinned** size, but the prune path fills it from `Version.size`, which is **plaintext** bytes. The gap is fixed and computable (40 B per sealed leaf, plus the root block). A pending-reclaim total built on the wrong unit is the same misreport in a new place. Derive the pinned total from the leaf count and root size rather than reusing the plaintext number.
- **#851 — partially already fixed; check before you write.** The ticket claimed `keep_latest` admits zero at `retention.rs:72-73`. That is stale in two ways. `RetentionPolicy::KeepLatest(NonZeroU64)` **already exists** (`crates/engine/src/content/retention.rs:65`), with the doc stating the zero state is unrepresentable rather than guarded. The hole survives only on the free function: `plan_prune(versions_newest_first: &[ContentVersion], keep_latest: usize)` at `retention.rs:93` still takes a plain `usize` and `skip(0)` still yields the whole history including the live version. Close that one signature; do not re-do the enum.

**One op that ends at publish, plus a retire ledger that is not an op** (#852). Both alternatives put a garbage-collection call on the critical path of user work: one op with two legs holds the FIFO head so the next rename waits on cleanup, and two ops repeats that plus a sixth `OpKind` with vacuous rebase semantics.

**The ledger stores roots; leaves are re-derived** at drain time via `decode_root` — plaintext det-CBOR, no key. That is three orders of magnitude smaller, and it is the irrecoverable half: once the publish lands nothing readable references the dropped roots, while leaves always can be recovered from a root.

**Leaves before root, versions oldest-first.** The journaled root **is** the expansion key, so retiring it first makes its leaf list unnameable and those bytes charged forever. Oldest-first is what `plan_prune` already emits — `PrunePlan.retire_targets` is documented "oldest first" (`content/retention.rs:82`) and the plan is built by iterating the doomed suffix in reverse (`content/retention.rs:99-103`) — and it leaves a valid suffix of history. Together these make the drain resumable across restart with nothing journaled but roots.

**Entries clear only on the server's own done-signal** — a batch reporting `retired: 0`, which is positive evidence and also covers the succeeded-but-response-lost case. Everything else backs off forever: **no attempt budget, no gave-up list, no dead-letter class.** Every failure is either self-clearing (offline, 401, a 429 from the registry throttle, a 503 from lock contention) or ours (a 400 from a bad CID we emitted, an unfetchable root we are charging for), and in every case the only user action is `Command::ManualRefresh`, which already exists.

**Owed bytes ride the entry** as one `u64` from `ContentVersion.size_bytes` — in the corrected pinned unit, per the folded-in #850 — and surface as a **vault-level pending-reclaim figure** beside the quota, the ticket's own missing "record of what was owed".

**Mode-derived legs, bytes tracking hosted.** Hosted to hosted, External to provider, Dual to both; the byte figure drains on hosted confirmation. External accounts hold **size-zero rows** (`register()` records membership at size 0, hosted ingress refused for BYO, `content.service.ts:246-253`), so a hosted-only ledger would self-satisfy instantly in External mode.

**A distinct `RetireLedger` seam** with its own conformance kit, on `FloorStore`'s precedent. It diverges from the op queue on lifetime, ordering (a set, not a FIFO), failure contract (never-discard versus dead-letter) and cancellability at once. Reusing the op queue is cheaper and inherits #832's owner tag free, but it puts a non-FIFO non-cancellable record in a store whose cold-start sweep **deletes** what it cannot decode.

**Owner-scoping is forced, not tidy.** Account A's owed CIDs retried under account B's token delete no rows, return `retired: 0`, and satisfy the done-signal without reclaiming anything.

## Harvest reference

`apps/api/src/ipfs/pending-unpin/` on branch `v1` is the same shape server-side: a durable outbox drained in ordered batches, per-row failure isolation ("leave row for next run; do not abort the batch"), a refcount-then-unpin helper, and a depth gauge. v1 could place it server-side only because it called Kubo `pin/ls` directly; v2 cannot, since no endpoint lists an account's pin rows (#826).

## Acceptance

- `plan_prune` cannot be called with a zero keep-count — unrepresentable, not guarded.
- `reclaimed_bytes` equals the sum of the sizes the retire call actually frees, in pinned bytes.
- A pruned 1 GiB version retires across multiple `REGISTRY_BATCH_MAX` batches, leaves before root, and is resumable after a mid-drain restart.
- A retire returning `retired: 0` clears the entry; every other failure retries.
- The pending-reclaim figure drains to zero on hosted confirmation and never on an External-only leg.

## Gate

`Engine Tests`, `Contract Suite`.

Yes, though the value is narrower than "making progress" — it's specifically about the one resource that's serialized.

The review queue is the long pole: five PRs at one slot an hour is ~5 hours minimum, and that cost is unavoidable whenever we pay it. CI isn't a long pole — once Actions recovers, all five run in parallel. So reviews done during the outage are hours we don't spend after it, and every hour we sit idle is a slot destroyed for nothing. Findings are also fixable right now, since the Rust gates all run locally.

The honest caveats:

**Nothing ships either way today** — you're right about that. This only front-loads.

**A rebase after each merge changes the head**, so a review obtained now technically covers a commit that won't be the merged one. For these PRs that's near-zero risk — the rebases so far have been clean and I verify the committed tree each time — but it's not literally the same bytes.

**If a review lands findings, fixing them is fine, but re-verifying is partly blind** until CI returns. Local `cargo` gates cover the Rust PRs well; #1122 and #1117 lean more on CI.

My call is to keep going — it converts dead time into the only work that can't be parallelized later. But it's a genuine judgment call, not an obvious win, and if you'd rather not have PRs sitting ready through an outage I'll stop it and we resume clean when Actions is back.

**#1119 — 3 nitpicks, all three worth taking**, fixed in `1327e2c90` (push retrying, local network is flaky).

The one that mattered most was the **symmetry gap in `revoke_invite_link`**. Its doc comment claims *"a tag that is merely committed belongs to some grantee and is not this function's to cut"* — but the code only checked the tag was present in the commitment. It never confirmed the tag re-derives from the owner's secret and that record's own ephemeral key, which `convert_invite_claim` does at `:529`. So the stated rule wasn't enforced, and an owner-side record mix-up could cut an ordinary grantee's entry.

CodeRabbit rated it defense-in-depth. I'd put it slightly higher: a doc comment asserting an invariant the code doesn't check is how the *next* change reasons wrongly.

**I proved the new check bites rather than trusting it.** The existing `unknown.link` test passes through the commitment lookup, so it says nothing about the re-derivation. I added the case that isolates it — a record carrying another grantee's *committed* tag with its own ephemeral key — then deleted the check and confirmed that assertion goes red, and restored it green. Without that, I'd have shipped a check no test exercises.

The other two: a test for the ambiguous-link refusal (two records sharing one ephemeral identity must refuse, not resolve to first match), and a vacuity guard on the transport leak scan — `windows()` yields nothing when the payload is shorter than the needle, so all three "no plaintext in the clear" assertions could pass without scanning anything. That's the false-all-clear shape that's bitten this repo repeatedly.

Full gates green: fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, the whole engine suite, and the wasm32 target check.

**Two left: #1122, then #1117.**

**ALWAYS prefix `gh` with `env -u GITHUB_TOKEN`.** Leave the primary checkout on `main` when you finish.

## The situation

PR #1118 (FUSE ranged read + plaintext chunk cache) **merged to `main`**. PR #1123 (conditional edit / write clobber) is rebased onto that `main` and is red.

Failing test: `published::the_first_read_invalidates_the_kernels_data_cache_for_the_inode` at `crates/fuse/tests/fuse_op_core.rs:1252`, failing with `expected a data invalidation for ino 2, got []`. It is **green on `main`** and **red on #1123's branch** — I reproduced both locally, so this is a genuine interaction, not flake and not a rebase mistake.

Work on the PR branch:
```
git fetch origin fix/conditional-edit-rebase
git checkout -B rb-1123 origin/fix/conditional-edit-rebase
cargo test -p cipherbox-fuse --test fuse_op_core   # reproduces
```
Do NOT rebase; it is already on current `main`.

## What I have established

`crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:305-315` decides whether to tell the kernel its page cache is stale:

```rust
let before = self.projected_content(open.node).await?;
let stream = self.engine.open_content_stream(open.node).await?;
if !self.handles.attach_stream(handle, stream) { ... }
// Opening the stream verified a head version the kernel's page cache
// for this inode may predate.
if self.projected_content(open.node).await? != before {
    let ino = self.inodes.ino_for(open.node);
    self.adapter.invalidate(Invalidation::Data { ino });
```

So #1118 infers "the kernel may be stale" **indirectly**, from the engine's projected content changing across the stream open. #1123 changed how the write plane projects head versions — its own report says "the drain projects the head its own publishes established via `project_child_version`" — and it touches `crates/engine/src/facade.rs`, `sync/rebase.rs`, `sync/drain.rs`.

My hypothesis, which you must verify rather than assume: #1123 makes the projection already correct *before* the stream opens, so `before == after`, the branch never fires, and the kernel is never invalidated.

## What I need you to work out

**The central question: is the invalidation still needed, and is #1118's before/after heuristic still a sound way to detect it?**

Consider carefully — the kernel's page cache staleness is a property of what the *kernel* holds, which is independent of whether the *engine's* projection happened to change across those two calls. If #1123 makes the projection accurate earlier, the hazard #1118 guards against may still exist while its detector has gone silent. That would be a **latent stale-read in the real mount**, not merely a broken test. Equally, it is possible the invalidation genuinely is unnecessary in this path now — but you must prove that from the code, not assert it.

- The detector is now wrong and must key off something that actually tracks kernel-visible staleness.
- The test's setup no longer reproduces the condition it means to, and the test should be re-aimed at the real hazard.
- Something else the code shows you.

## Diagnosis

The old detector inferred kernel-cache staleness from the **engine's projection** moving across the stream open, at `crates/fuse/src/ops.rs:305-315` (pre-fix):

```rust
let before = self.projected_content(open.node).await?;   // (size, mtime)
let stream = self.engine.open_content_stream(open.node).await?;
if self.projected_content(open.node).await? != before { /* Invalidation::Data */ }
```

Your hypothesis is correct, and I confirmed it causally rather than by inspection. Instrumenting `stream_for` on the branch:

- with `#1123`'s new `project_child_version(...)` in `publish_new_file` (`crates/engine/src/sync/drain.rs:1175-1185`): `before=(Some(200), Some(0))`, `after=(Some(200), Some(0))` → silent
- with that one call disabled (i.e. `main`'s behaviour): `before=(None, None)`, `after=(Some(200), Some(0))` → fires, test green

So on `main` the test passed because the projection was **incomplete**, not because the kernel was stale. On a freshly-minted inode the kernel holds nothing, so that repaint was spurious to begin with.

**It is a latent stale-read, not just a broken test.** The projection moving is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence about the kernel. Anything that advances the projection without the mount serving bytes silences the detector — and `main`'s `publish_update_content` already did exactly that (it set `node.mtime`/`node.size` inline; #1123 replaced those lines with `project_child_version` at `drain.rs:1567`). So the false negative already existed on `main` for local **edits**; #1123 extended the same shape to **creates** and thereby knocked out the test that had been passing incidentally.

The poll path does **not** refresh child content (`project_folder` copies `size`/`mtime`/`content_version`/`head_content_cid` from the prior snapshot and never re-reads a child body), so a remote publish still trips the old heuristic — which is why the interaction only surfaces on the local-write path.

## What I changed

Key the repaint to what the mount **actually served**, which is the only thing the kernel's pages can have come from:

- `crates/engine/src/facade.rs` — added `Engine::stream_version_cid(handle) -> Option<Vec<u8>>`, the `contentCid` of the version a live stream pinned. Rust-only, no wasm/TS surface.
- `crates/fuse/src/ops.rs` — `OperationCore` keeps `streamed: HashMap<NodeId, Vec<u8>>`; `stream_for` invalidates when a bind lands on a version different from the last one bound for that node. A first bind repaints nothing. Cleared on `unmount`. `projected_content` deleted with its last caller.
- `crates/fuse/src/ops.rs` — added `OperationCore::engine_mut()`. The mount takes ownership of the engine, and the distinguishing scenario is unreachable without driving the same session's write plane (a second engine over one account is not the same hazard). This is the one piece of new surface I'd flag for your judgement.

## Test: I changed what is asserted

`the_first_read_invalidates_the_kernels_data_cache_for_the_inode` asserted that the **first** read repaints. That is no longer the claim — the kernel holds nothing for an inode this session minted and never served — so I replaced it rather than adjusting it:

- `a_read_off_a_version_the_mount_never_served_repaints_the_kernels_data_cache` — reads A, publishes a new version through the mounted engine, reads again, requires `Invalidation::Data`. It additionally asserts `getattr` is byte-identical either side of the second open, which bakes the anti-vacuity argument into the test itself: the projection delta is empty, so only the served version can separate the two reads.
- `reading_the_version_already_served_repaints_nothing` — first bind, later window off a pinned stream, and a fresh handle on the same head all stay silent.

I deliberately did **not** add a remote-writer variant: the mechanism is identical (a bind on a different version) and it passes under both detectors, so it would not have guarded anything.

Reverting `stream_for` to the projection-delta heuristic: **40 passed, 1 failed** — `expected a data invalidation for ino 2, got []`. Restored: **41 passed, 0 failed**.

- **No `blueprint/desktop.md` edit.** Line 229 already specifies that a background reconcile should drive push-invalidation off the engine event stream. That path is not built, and my change is about the stream-bind path only — the stated design is unchanged.

Fixed and pushed (`51f23e6a7`), with every gate verified **unpiped** this time: `typecheck=0`, `lint=0`, `build=0`, client tests 386 passing.

**That failure was mine, and worth naming.** I claimed `FetchEventLike` already declared `waitUntil` — it didn't; line 42's optional `waitUntil?` belongs to `PortMessageEventLike`. My local typecheck reported 0 because I piped it through `tail`, so `$?` was `tail`'s exit code. That is exactly the trap I put in the brief for all eight wave-6 agents, and I walked into it myself while verifying someone else's work. CI caught it; my local check was worthless.

The fix is one line — declaring `waitUntil?` on `FetchEventLike` — and the underlying finding stands.

## #1123's semantic conflict: worse than a broken test

The delegated investigation proved it causally rather than by inspection, instrumenting both configurations:

- with #1123's `project_child_version` in `publish_new_file`: `before=(Some(200), Some(0))`, `after=(Some(200), Some(0))` → **silent**
- with that one call disabled (i.e. `main`): `before=(None, None)`, `after=(Some(200), Some(0))` → fires

So **on `main` the test passed because the projection was incomplete, not because the kernel was stale.** On a freshly-minted inode the kernel holds nothing, so that repaint was spurious to begin with.

And the false negative already existed on `main` for local *edits* — `publish_update_content` set `mtime`/`size` inline, silencing the same detector. #1123 merely extended the shape to creates and knocked over the test that had been passing incidentally.

The fix keys the repaint to **what the mount actually served** (`Engine::stream_version_cid`), which is the only thing the kernel's pages can have come from, rather than to a projection delta that is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence about the kernel. Both replacement tests were mutation-checked.

I tightened one thing after review: `engine_mut` was public API with only a test caller, now `#[doc(hidden)]` per the `crates/core/src/kdf` precedent.

The three that qualify all changed **behavior after the verdict**, not just prose:

- **#1119** is the strongest case. The fix adds a fail-closed check on the revoke path — re-deriving the record's tag so a record from another scope root can't cut an ordinary grantee's entry. It's a new crypto invariant in a trust boundary, and AGENTS.md makes `/crypto-privacy-review` mandatory for exactly this. CR reviewed the PR *without* that guard existing.
- **#1123** is the semantic-conflict repair, not a CR finding at all — it replaced the projection-delta staleness detector with one keyed to `Engine::stream_version_cid`, and exposed new engine surface to do it. That's the largest unreviewed behavior delta in the wave.

#1117's post-review commit is the type declaration that fixed the `TS2339` CI break — no runtime change; the substantive `waitUntil` fix at `055ed62a5` *was* reviewed.

**#1119 is clean but stale.** It's re-reviewed and ready, but it still sits on the pre-#1120 main and will need a rebase once #1123 lands. Nothing to do until then — flagging so the clean verdict doesn't get mistaken for merge-ready-right-now.
